caseno: Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 9954 of 2006 with Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 11080 of 2006.
lawyer:
Rokanuddin Mahmud with Sheikh Hasan Arif, Advocates------ For the Petitioners. 
MA Muntakim, Advocate-For the Informant------ Opposite Party.
parties:
AKM Iftekhar Ahmed and another ------ Petitioners
vs
State ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Sharifuddin Chaklader J: These two Rules were issued at the instance of the accused petitioners for quashment of the proceedings of Fatullah PS Case No. 125 dated 27-4-2006 pending in the Court of Magistrate, First Class, Narayanganj (South). 

 2. The facts relating for disposal of these two Rules are that the informant, an exporter of garments products, opened two fire insurance policies with Eastern Insurance Company Ltd where the petitioner, AKM Iftekhar Ahmed is Managing Director, and petitioner, AKM Mustafizur Rahman is Senior Vice President, (Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 9954 of 2006) and Md Habib Jamal, petitioner of Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 11080 of 2006 is the Company's Secretary of the aforesaid Insurance Company. A fire broke out on 16-2-2006 causing heavy damage to the factory. The informant demanded policy money to which the accused petitioner made proposal to negotiate and made a proposal to the effect that instead of paying Taka five crore as demanded, they are ready to pay Taka one crore. This, according to the informant, is violation of the trust and thus lodged the first information report. 

 3. Before entering into the merit of the case, we are to settle a question as has been raised from the side of the informant that the Rule in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 9954 of 2006 cannot be heard on merit and it should be discharged on the ground that the accused petitioners are fugitive from justice. It is a settled principle of law that fugitive from justice cannot claim any protection of law. To substantiate the claim, the informant filed an application for addition of party disclosing how the accused petitioners became fugitive from justice. 

 6. It appears from the cause title of the Rule petition that the accused persons were described written by hand and not typed as "present in Court". From the prayer portion of the said petition it appears that the accused petitioners prayed for "enlarge the petitioners on ad-interim bail" and this also was written by hand, not typed. The description made in the cause title and prayer made for bail is totally contradictory. It also appears from the order sheets annexed with the affidavit, that, despite granting several adjournments on the prayer of the learned Advocates for the accused petitioners for filing counter-affidavit, to controvert the allegation of being fugitive they did not file any counter-affidavit. It further appears that earlier, the accused petitioners obtained anticipatory bail in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 6238 of 2006 till filing of the charge sheet. When charge sheet was submitted, the petitioners did not surrender before the Court, as such, the learned Magistrate passed order on 2-7-2006 cancelling the bail of the accused petitioners and then issued warrant of arrest. It appears that accused petitioners without appearing or surrendering before the learned Magistrate, appeared before this Court upon concealing the fact that their bail was cancelled and that there was an order of warrant of arrest issued against them and made the aforesaid false statement and illegal prayer for bail. It is very unfortunate that the learned Advocate for the petitioners moved this Court and obtained the Rule, order of stay and bail by suppressing the fact that the bail of the accused petitioners were cancelled and there was an order of warrant of arrest hanging against the accused petitioners. 

 7. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, learned Advocate, appearing for the accused petitioners, at the first instance, submits on the merit of the Rule. According to him, the claim of insurance policy is always a subject matter of civil dispute for which no criminal case can be initiated, the informant having filed civil suit for recovery of the insured money, the proceeding under sections 406/420 of the Penal Code is liable to be quashed. 

 8. On the question of being fugitive from justice, as raised by the learned Advocate for the informant, Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Advocate, took time for filing an affidavit but when the matter was posted for delivery of judgment on the date fixed on 21-3-2007, 28-3-2007 and 3-4-2007 on the prayer of the learned Advocate, no affidavit was filed. The Court, however, for ends of justice, kept the delivery of judgment in abeyance till 21-3-2007 but in vain. Thereafter, the delivery of judgment was adjourned till 28-3-2007 and there- after, till 3-4-2007 and this Court was waiting with expectation that at least Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud would appear and enlighten us on the question as to whether the accused petitioners are fugitive or not, but unfortunately, none appeared to assist. The learned Advocate for the petitioners did not turn up to make any oral submission by filing an affidavit on the question whether the accused petitioners are fugitive or not. Today i.e. 4-4-2007, when the case is taken up for delivery of judgment, while we are delivering the judgment, none from the side of the accused petitioners were found present in Court. 

 9. We have perused the petitions under section 561A of the Code along with annexures. It appears from the petition in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 9954 of 2006 that there are some falsities In It. From the cause title of the same we find that the names, addresses and description of petitioners were 'typed' but after describing the same whereabouts of the accused petitioners have been described as "present in Court" by hand after penning through the typed words "on bail." But same is neither initialed by affidavit-commissioner nor has been corrected with the leave of the Court. In the body of the petition no where it has disclosed whether the accused petitioners are on bail but in prayer portion, after the prayer for staying the proceeding of the concerned case, we find a prayer has been inserted by pen "enlarge the petitioners on ad-interim bail" which, of course, contains an initial on the left hand column. On perusal of the said initial, it appears that the same does not tally with the other initials of the affidavit-commissioner made on the same page and also on other pages. 

 12. In the case of Khalilur Rahman vs State, relied on an unreported decision of the Special Bench dated l3-4-1978 passed in Criminal Appeal No. 472 of 1968, that is, the case of Nirmal Krishna Chanda vs State, reported in 33 DLR 12, a Division Bench of this Court held that a fugitive from justice is not entitled to any relief. In the decision of Nurun Nahar Zaman vs State and another, reported in 1995 BLD 537 it has been held that: 

 13. In the case of MA Wahab, Advocate vs State, reported in 1990 BLD (AD) 50 = 42 DLR (AD) 223 it has been held in paragraphs 7 and 8 as follows: 

 8. We do not like to pursue the matter further and hope that there will not be a second occasion for us to feel unhappy as we did feel in the present case. The learned Deputy Attorney-General, who appeared for the State, submitted that the paragraphs in question are not essential for maintaining the order cancelling the bail of the appellants." 

 14. In the case of Saidur Rahman alias Chan Miah and others vs State, reported in 40 DLR (AD) 281, it has been held that: 

 "Since, however, the appellants were not covered by a legal order of interim bail, the proper order the learned judge ought to have passed and which is always usually passed in such cases was to direct the appellants to surrender within a certain time before taking up the petition of appeal for hearing." 

 15. In the decisions reported in 49 DLR 100 : 1997 BLD 235 (Dr Ahmed Sharif vs State) and 1998 BLD (AD) 227 : 3 BLC (AD) 171 (Moulana Md Yusuf vs State) it has been held that when the petitioner flouted summons and warrant and never asked for bail, it is difficult to entertain his application for quashment before surrender to the Court. In the case of Moulana Md Yousuf vs State and another; reported in 3 BLC (AD) 171, it has been held that it is more important than anything else to put the matter on a legal keel. A Magistrate's Court at Gopalganj has taken cognisance rightly or wrongly of the offence under sections 295A and 298 of the Penal Code and reported summons and warrant of arrest has been issued against the respondent for his appearance. The respondent is certainly at liberty to question the authority of the Magistrate to take cognisance of the offences alleged but before doing so there is an obligation cast upon the accused to show obedience to the order of the Court for appearance. It is true that the accused was a Professor of Dhaka University and one of the intellectuals of the country but this does not absolve him of the responsibility to appear before a Court and asking for bail. 

 17. Since we find the accused petitioners are fugitives from justice, it is not necessary to discuss the merit of the case. 

 18. In the result, the Rule of Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 9954 of 2006 is discharged, 

 20. The Rule of Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 11080 of 2006: we find that just after obtaining the bail the accused petitioner rushed to this Court without waiting for framing of charge or invoking the provisions of section 241A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. These are the duty of the learned Magistrate not of the High Court Division; High Court Division is not an 'ass' to bear all the burden of the learned Magistrate. It has been settled in the decisions reported in 50 DLR (AD) 115, 48 DLR 102, 50 DLR 301, 50 DLR 551, 2000 BLD (AD) 50 that in order to relieve the burden of the High Court Division with frivolous cases, sections 241A and 265C were included in the Code of Criminal Procedure for enabling the accused persons to place their cases before the learned Magistrate or trial Court in order to come out of the proceeding. It has already been settled in a number of cases that a case cannot be quashed on defence materials. Reliance may be made in the case reported in 48 DLR (AD) 213 where it has been held that a criminal case can be quashed only on prosecution materials. It has already been settled by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the decisions reported in 15 DLR (SC) 150 upto 1992 BLD 627 that when there is alternative remedy available to the accused person, section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not available to the accused person. The statements of Rule petition are his defence case for quashment of the same, the accused petitioner neither invoked the provision of section 241A of the Code of Criminal Procedure nor waited till framing of charge. From a reading of the FIR it appears that some involvement of the accused petitioner was disclosed therein. In this case police has not yet submitted report. It has been settled in several decisions that quashment at such earlier stage is not permissible in law. 

 21. In the result, the Rule of Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 11080 of 2006 is discharged. 

 26. We have already mentioned earlier the case of MA Wahab, Advocate vs State, reported in 2000 BLD (AD) 50: 42 DLR (AD) 223. 

 "Attorneys and Advocates who appear to present petitions on the criminal side other than those which lie as of right are under a duty to see that they are acting in furtherance of justice. It seems to us that this duty is clearly violated when aid, for securing interference by this Court with a judicial order, is given by these officers of the Court to persons who, to their knowledge, are in contempt, i.e. as fugitives from justice, without at the same time ensuring that such persons conform to the judicial orders applicable to them. In the present case, the mini- mum requirement, in relation to this Court, was that the Attorney should have taken steps to secure the appearance of the petitioner before this Court on the first day when the petition came up for hearing. He may, at the same time, have moved, through Counsel, for an order suspending execution of the High Court sentence. The course adopted by the Attorney in the present case was, in our opinion, not in accordance with his proper duty." 

 28. 'In the case of Aziza Khatun vs State. reported in 19 DLR 354 their Lordships observed as: 

 29. In the case of State vs Khandker Shamsul Huq, reported in 19 DLR 526, their Lordships were of the opinion: 

 "Lawyers as they are, they are the very limbs of the administration of justice. The standard of care as owed by them to the Court and to the unhampered administration of justice is very much higher than that expected from the layman. They are not mere conduit-pipes for passing on to Court whatever is whispered in their ears by their lay clients wishfully, to further their cause. In the present case, there is nothing to indicate that their clients even, who are laymen, could have dreamt of such a ground. The scandalous expressions having occurred in the ground itself, the liability at all events is entirely that of the lawyers responsible for the drafting and the moving thereof in Court. 

 30. In similar situation as that of the instant case i.e. the lawyer being absent while the appeal was taken up for hearing, the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Asif Ali vs State reported in 25 DLR (SC) 68 was of the opinion "while the learned members of the Bar appearing in cases as officers of the Courts are entitled to all genuine consideration and accommodation in conducting proceedings before the Courts consistently with the onerous responsibilities of the Court itself to discharge its duties diligently and conscientiously, it is impossible to concede that the learned Counsels should be allowed to regulate the work or the proceedings in the Court, according to their own choice to suit their own convenience." 

 31. In the case of Rashid Murtuza Qureshi vs State, reported in 17 DLR (SC) 608 where the appellant, an Advocate, was proceeded for contempt of Court for gesturing indecent behaviour to the learned High Court Judge while the learned Judge was in his chamber. There it has been observed that "Although proceedings in chamber are not invested with the full formality of those that take place in Court, yet the circumstances in which, and the attitude with which an interruption is made even in chamber proceedings are factors which may deprive the interruption of all innocence in the light of con- tempt' of Court's authority and dignity." Although the Supreme Court exonerated the appellant in appeal but concluded with "he should nerve forget that however important in substance or principle a matter may be which he is placing before the Court, he should never forget that his own dignity as a lawyer obliges him to place it before the Court in the manner of a submission, couched in the traditional language of courtesy that is due to the Court. 

 32. In the case of State vs Abdul Gafun reported in 13  DLR 851 it is observed that "lawyers should exercise great care and caution in drafting and pleading in Court an. application which contains allegations reflecting upon the integrity of the Court. They owe a duty not merely to their clients but also to the Court of which they are trusted officers. They enjoy a good deal of privilege, and also not an inconsiderable latitude from the Court, in the exercise of their professional duties. Whereas they should boldly and fearlessly advocate the cause of their clients, they should re-member that it is their paramount duty to maintain the dignity and integrity of the Court itself. It has, therefore, been the time honored tradition of the Bar that it constitutes itself as the staunchest defender against an unjustified attack upon the Court which they are called upon to assist in the administration of justice. It should also be realised that the generality of those engaged in dispensing justice, by the very nature of their calling, live in comparative aloofness and are, therefore, in a disadvantageous position in defending themselves, in their cloistered seclusion, from irresponsible and extraneous onslaughts on their integrity." 

 33. In the case of Mohammad Ayub Khan vs Custodian of Evacue Property, reported in 15 DLR (WP) 93 it has been observed "an Advocate does not discharge his duty with due regard of the responsibility of his high office if he uses derogatory instructions which can be verified by him to be false, by ordinary exercise of care. It is necessary for maintaining an atmosphere of mutual trust between the Court and an Advocate that the Advocate should not even state his inferences as fact. As the Court has a right to listen to a Counsel with confidence, their' trust is not respected if he makes grossly exaggerated, misleading or irresponsible statements. 

 34. in the case of State vs Delwar Hossain, reported in 12 DLR 613, it was observed that members of the Bar should remember that their primary duty is to the Bench and then to their clients...............it is the duty of the lawyer to uphold the prestige and honour of the Court........: 

 35. In the case of State vs M Noman, reported in 16 DLR393, where when on an application filed by late lamented MH Khandker, a well respected Senior Advocate, for transferring a Writ petition from the Court of Mr Justice Imam Hossain Chowdhury, CJ, Mr Noman, an officiating Chief Engineer, Mr MH Khandker and Mr Shafiqur Rahman, Advocates were punished for contempt of Court, by a Special Bench constituted for hearing of the contempt matter arisen from, amongst others, on an application for transfer of the Writ petition. The punishment was upheld by the Supreme Court of Pakistan (18 DLR (SC) 124) upon holding that there is no provision in law for transfer of a case from a Bench of the High Court except the one in section 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It was further held that "Judges are protected from Civil or Criminal Process if they, in the discharge of their judicial duty, act in good faith" and "Advocates are officers of the, Court; they are not 'entitled to a protection greater than the protection available to Judges. Professional privilege is conceded to an  Advocate only on the ground of public policy, so that they may pursue their client's cause without any fear of penalty' and "Advocates, in the discharge of their duty, must act in good faith as is required by the 9th Exception to section 449 of the Penal Code and must not say or do anything which might cause hurt to the Court itself as an institution. 

 36. The Supreme Court of India in the matter of 'A' an Advocate, reported in AIR 1962 Supreme Couri1337, was of the view, "he has in this Court, condemned himself, as a liar' and as one who is either ignorant of the elementary rules of professional ethics or has no regard for them. In our opinion, the Advocate has mischosen his profession." The Indian Supreme Court affirmed the punishment holding that "let him learn that a lawyer must never be a liar." 

 38. We have already mentioned earlier that by inserting some information in the petition by hand-writing upon penning through the typed words "on bail" without the same being countersigned, initialed or making any declaration with the leave of the Court', the learned Advocates for the petitioners committed an offence of perjury and professional misconduct. We have also found that by making the statement "on present in Court" and concealing the fact that the accused petitioner's bail have been cancelled and warrant-of arrest is hanging against them, the learned Advocates not only misled the Court in issuing the Rule but also committed a professional misconduct by practicing fraud upon the Court, which is punishable under, the law of the land. We are ashamed to find that a Senior Lawyer defended the petitioners who, under the facts and circumstances stated above, are fugitives from justice which is not only unethical .but also condemnable. 

 From the aforesaid citations and provisions of statute it appears that lawyer's foremost duty is to uphold the dignity, honour and prestige of the Court and must place the client's case with clean hands. There was a time when there was values of the learned Advocates before Court as well as before the public hut the said values gradually evaporated when we find the high-sounding Advocates take servile attitude towards their highly positioned clients, both monied and political, and in order to give them relief by any means, act disgracefully inside Court. If this position be continued, I am afraid a day will come when practically there will be no legal system in Bangladesh.
